name: Thakali
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Thakali (thak1245) is not in the catalog. The single title hit, Pittman 1970 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies' (Part II of the 1970 Tone Systems report, full djvu text already on file), was read in full: it is a comparative register/tone paper giving Thakali word-bases four pitch/voice-quality classes (clear high level, clear extra-high falling, breathy low rising-falling, breathy low level) and says nothing about word-stress placement in Thakali (its 'stressed/unstressed' labels are Tamang). Beyond the title hit: Hari & Maibaum 1970 Appendix A/B (on file, read) describe a morpheme-level tone/register system and only utterance-level intonational stress; Sharma 2008 'Thakali language: A phonemic overview' (Nepalese Linguistics 23, fetched sources today, text layer) has no stress statement and defers to Hari 1970 for tone; Sharma 2006 (on file, scanned) is silent. Not obtainable: Hari 1970 'Thakali tone and higher levels' (Part I, ERIC ED046001 'PDF pending restoration', not on archive.org; HathiTrust/Google Books blocked) — the highest-priority acquisition, since the ERIC abstract says Part I analyses 'stress group' and foot-nucleus units; Georg 1996 Marphatan Thakali and Regmi et al. 2010 A grammar of Thakali are print-only (medium priority).org, ERIC, Digital Himalaya's Nepalese Linguistics ToC and Glottolog. new_statements.quote: Phonetically we have also to distinguish between high and low pitch. This is however conditioned by the vowel quality as follows: Breathy vowels always have low pitch, and clear vowels in the corresponding position always have high pitch. But within each of these two categories we have a phonemic contrast between level pitch and contour pitch. These features, however, are not a characteristic of the syllable, but of the morpheme. [...] (Intonational stress is realized as a pitch upstep and general intensity on the stressed syllable.)
new_statements.citation: Hari, Annemarie & Anita Maibaum. 1970. Thakali texts. In F. K. Lehman (ed.), Occasional Papers of the Wolfenden Society on Tibeto-Burman Linguistics, Vol. III: Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal (Hale & Pike, eds.), Part III: Texts I, pp. 165-306. Urbana: University of Illinois.
new_statements.locator: Appendix A §3 'Tone', p. 293 (first quote); Appendix B 'Punctuation', p. 294 (second quote)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Thakali is described as a pitch/tone language: each morpheme carries one of four prosodies (clear high level, clear extra-high falling, breathy low level, breathy low rising-falling), pitch register being conditioned by breathy vs clear vowels and the level-vs-contour contrast being phonemic at the morpheme level; clear level affixes are atonic and take their pitch from the stem. Stress is treated only as an intonational (utterance-level) feature realized as pitch upstep plus intensity, e.g. a heavy stress on the last syllable of the utterance under certain intonation patterns and on the first syllable of a question word; no word-level stress position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords add voiced stops and a nasalized vowel; irregularities in tone are not discussed in the opened pages.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is stated to be a property of the morpheme (word-base), with tonic/atonic affixes; 'stress' in the source is intonational and belongs to the utterance (phrase) level, described through punctuation symbols used in the texts. Preliminary SIL field analysis (1969-70), presented as a summary appended to a text collection rather than a full phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Hari & Maibaum 1970) is SIL work on the Thakali of the Thak Khola (texts include the Tulachan clan legend and a trip to the Thak Khola; Sharma 2006 divides Thakali into Tukuche, Marphatan and Syang dialects, differing in 'tone and pitch'); the opened pages do not name the dialect explicitly. Georg 1996 describes the Marpha village variety ('Marphatan Thakali', listed by Glottolog as an alternative name under thak1245, no separate glottocode). All are treated under thak1245.

This is however conditioned by the vowel quality as follows: Breathy vowels always have low pitch, and clear vowels in the corresponding position always have high pitch. But within each of these two categories we have a phonemic contrast between level pitch and contour pitch. These features, however, are not a characteristic of the syllable, but of the morpheme. [p. 293] ... (Intonational stress is realized as a pitch upstep and general intensity on the stressed syllable.) [p. 294]
new_statements.citation: Hari, Anna Maria & Anita Maibaum (1970). Thakali texts. In F. K. Lehman (ed.), Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal, Part III: Texts I, Appendix A 'Summary of the phonemic analysis as it relates to the orthography used', §3 Tone, p. 293; Appendix B 'Punctuation', p. 294. Urbana: University of Illinois.
new_statements.locator: Appendix A §3 Tone (p. 293) and Appendix B (p. 294)
new_statements.reading: The only first-hand prosodic description of Thakali readable in this sweep. It describes word prosody as a morpheme-level tone/register system (clear vs breathy, level vs contour pitch; clear level affixes atonic, taking the stem's pitch) and describes 'stress' only as an utterance-level intonational feature (pitch upstep + intensity), placed by intonation pattern, typically on the last syllable of the utterance. It states no lexical word-stress rule, so for a stress catalog Thakali should be coded from this as a tone/register language with no reported word stress (silent on fixed placement), pending Hari 1970 Part I.

sources.quote: Phonetically we have also to distinguish between high and low pitch. This is however conditioned by the vowel quality as follows: Breathy vowels always have low pitch, and clear vowels in the corresponding position always have high pitch. But within each of these two categories we have a phonemic contrast between level pitch and contour pitch. These features, however, are not a characteristic of the syllable, but of the morpheme. [...] (Intonational stress is realized as a pitch upstep and general intensity on the stressed syllable.)
sources.locator: Appendix A §3 'Tone', p. 293 (first quote); Appendix B 'Punctuation', p. 294 (second quote)
sources.note: Pitch is conditioned by vowel register (breathy = low, clear = high) with a phonemic level-vs-contour contrast that is a property of the morpheme, not the syllable; affixes are tonic or atonic. Stress is mentioned only as 'intonational stress' (pitch upstep + intensity) placed by utterance-level intonation patterns (e.g. heavy stress on the last syllable of the utterance before ') ' or '!', on the first syllable of a question word); no word-stress placement rule is given.

sources.citation: Sharma (Gautam), Narayan P. (2008). Thakali language: A phonemic overview. Nepalese Linguistics 23: 355-370 (Digital Himalaya ToC prints 343-354).
sources.quote: It is basically a monosyllabic language. Most of the morphemes are formed of a single syllable. ... The study of tone on Thakali has been made in detail by Hari (1970). The Thakali tone system may be characterized in terms of two kinds of contrasts - contrasts for breathiness and contrast for pitch contour. The contrast between breathy and clear is relevant only to the onset of a morpheme while the pitch contour of a morpheme extends over the whole morpheme (Hari, 1970).
sources.locator: §6 Syllables and Syllabification, §7 Tone, pp. 367-369 (txt lines ~12189-12250)
sources.note: No mention of stress anywhere in the article (grep of the whole volume text: 'stress' occurs only in unrelated articles). Word prosody described as tone (breathiness + pitch contour), following Hari 1970. Also read Sharma 2006 (NL 22, scanned on file): silent on stress.

sources.quote: In the early fall of 1969, Maria Hari ... described Thakali word-bases as being either (a) clear high level, (b) clear extra-high falling, (c) breathy low rising-falling, or (d) breathy low level. ... words which are (a) high stressed in Tamang are clear intense in Gurung and clear high level in Thakali, (b) unstressed in Tamang are clear relaxed in Gurung and clear extra-high falling in Thakali, (c) mid stressed in Tamang are breathy rising in Gurung and breathy low rising-falling in Thakali, and (d) low stressed in Tamang are breathy low in Gurung and breathy low level in Thakali
sources.locator: Pittman chapter = djvu-text lines ~351-850 (printed pp. 1-8), esp. sections 2-3 and Table 3
sources.note: Reports Hari's (fall 1969) analysis: 'Thakali word-bases may be (a) clear high level, (b) clear extra-high falling, (c) breathy low rising-falling, or (d) breathy low level'; contrasts this with Tamang, whose four classes are defined by stress (high/mid/low stressed vs unstressed); states that 'Stress, relative pitch, pitch contour, intensity and breathiness carry a high proportion of the functional load of the register system in T[amang], Gu[rung], and Th[akali]'. No word-stress position for Thakali.
